```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)

setwd(here::here())

source("src/unzip_data.r")
source("src/apply_types.r")

dict_assessor <- read_csv("data/dictionary_assessor.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dict_deed <- read_csv("data/dictionary_deed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dict_avm <- read_csv("data/dictionary_avm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

data_assessor_month <- apply_types(data_assessor_month, dict_assessor)
data_deed <- apply_types(data_deed, dict_deed)
data_avm <- apply_types(data_avm, dict_avm)

if ("Fips" %in% names(data_avm) && !"FIPS" %in% names(data_avm)) {
  data_avm <- rename(data_avm, FIPS = Fips)
}

matched <- data_assessor_month |>
  filter(!is.na(CurrentSaleTransactionId)) |>
  inner_join(
    data_deed |> select(PropertyID, FATransactionID, SaleAmt),
    by = c("PropertyID" = "PropertyID",
      "CurrentSaleTransactionId" = "FATransactionID")
  ) |>
  inner_join(
    data_avm |> select(PropertyID, FinalValue),
    by = "PropertyID"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    deed_price = as.numeric(SaleAmt),
    avm_error = FinalValue - deed_price
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(deed_price) & deed_price > 0)
```

## Data Profile

I used `PropertyID` as the join key. It appears in most pairwise matches the same `PropertyID` appears in both datasets more than assessor's parcel number.

[insert table]

Deed data has non-unique `PropertyID`. I presume this is because some properties are transacted multiple times.

## Product

I was interested in how well the AVM predicts the sale price reported in the deed data, so the following is the mean absolute error of AVM compared to the sale price. Note that this matches both the deed and AVM datasets to only the monthly assessor data, since that merged better with the deed data (about 1/3 of rows).

```{r}
#| label: accuracy-table
median_price <- median(matched$deed_price, na.rm = TRUE)

both <- !is.na(matched$FinalValue) & !is.na(matched$deed_price)
errors <- matched$FinalValue[both] - matched$deed_price[both]
abs_errors <- abs(errors)

within_100k <- sum(abs(errors) <= 100000)
pct_within_100k <- 100 * within_100k / sum(both)

tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Properties compared",
    "Mean absolute error",
    "Mean absolute error (% of median sale price)",
    "Mean bias",
    "Within +/- $100,000",
    "Within +/- $100,000 (%)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    format(sum(both), big.mark = ","),
    scales::dollar(round(mean(abs_errors))),
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(abs_errors) / median_price),
    scales::dollar(round(mean(errors))),
    format(within_100k, big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_within_100k)
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

It looks the frequency of the deviation is slightly right-skewed, but it looks like three-quarters of values fall within +/- $100,000.

```{r}
#| label: bias-histogram
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(matched, aes(x = avm_error)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "AVM - Deed Sale Price",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Memo

I'm not sure where the AVM data is sourced, but I think it's important to produce predictions of price that are accurate. To be honest, the choice of analysis was also a function of time and the surface-level familiarity I had developed over an hour of looking at the data. 

The next step I would've done would be to fit a decision tree with an algorithm like random forest on the assesor dataset.
